Scotland's Lighthouse Routes by Motorcycle

Scotland has over 200 lighthouses, many built by the Stevenson family in the 18th and 19th centuries. These white towers stand on some of the most dramatic headlands in Britain, and riding to them takes you to the very edges of the Scottish coastline. Here are the routes worth making.

Northern Lighthouses

  • Cape Wrath Lighthouse: Britain's most northwesterly point. Not directly accessible by motorcycle (ferry and minibus required from Durness), but the ride to Durness through Sutherland is extraordinary.
  • Dunnet Head Lighthouse: The most northerly point of mainland Britain (not John o' Groats, as many believe). Ride the B855 to the headland for views across to Orkney. The lighthouse is a short walk from parking.
  • Strathy Point Lighthouse: On the north coast between Bettyhill and Melvich. A narrow road leads to the headland with Atlantic views in every direction.

West Coast Lighthouses

  • Neist Point Lighthouse, Skye: One of Scotland's most photographed lighthouses, perched on a dramatic clifftop on Skye's western tip. The walk down to the lighthouse from the car park is steep but spectacular.
  • Ardnamurchan Point Lighthouse: The most westerly point of mainland Britain. The B8007 to reach it is a narrow, twisting single-track road through remote wilderness — the ride is as memorable as the destination.
  • Mull of Kintyre Lighthouse: Made famous by Paul McCartney's song. The road down to the lighthouse is extremely steep and challenging — one of the most demanding roads in Scotland.

East Coast Lighthouses

  • Buchan Ness Lighthouse, Boddam: Scotland's most easterly mainland point. A compact lighthouse in a small fishing village.
  • Scurdie Ness, Montrose: A picturesque lighthouse at the mouth of the Montrose Basin. Good coastal riding to reach it.
  • Bell Rock Lighthouse: Not accessible by motorcycle (it's offshore!), but visible from Arbroath, and the Signal Tower Museum in Arbroath tells the incredible story of its construction.
Lighthouse roads lead to headlands — exposed, windswept points with no shelter. Be prepared for strong winds, especially if approaching from the west. The ride to a lighthouse is often on narrow, twisting roads with no barriers — ride within your limits and enjoy the journey.

Planning a Lighthouse Tour

  • Most lighthouses are automated and not open to visitors, but the grounds and views are freely accessible
  • A few lighthouses offer accommodation — staying in a lighthouse is a unique touring experience (see Northern Lighthouse Board for details)
  • Many lighthouse headlands have no phone signal — download offline maps
  • The roads to remote lighthouses are often single-track with passing places — allow extra time
  • Photography is rewarding at any time, but dawn and dusk light on white lighthouse towers is particularly stunning

Lighthouses mark the edge of the land. Riding to them takes you to places most people never visit — headlands where the road ends and the ocean begins. These are Britain's final frontiers, and they're magnificent. Read our Lighthouse Routes in England and Wales by Motorcycle guide for more. Read our Scottish Loch Circuits by Motorcycle: Ride Around Scotland's Finest Lochs guide for more.
keyTakeaways: Scotland has over 200 lighthouses, many built by the Stevenson family, on its most dramatic headlands.
Neist Point on Skye is one of the most photographed, reached by a steep walk from the car park.
The B8007 to Ardnamurchan Point, mainland Britain's most westerly spot, is a memorable single-track ride.
Dunnet Head, not John o' Groats, is the true northerly tip of mainland Britain, reached via the B855.
Lighthouse headlands are exposed and windswept, so prepare for strong winds and download offline maps.

faq.q: Can I ride right up to these lighthouses?
faq.a: Mostly you can reach a nearby car park, then walk the final stretch. Neist Point on Skye involves a steep walk down from parking, and Dunnet Head is a short walk from where you leave the bike. Cape Wrath is the exception, requiring a passenger ferry and minibus from Durness rather than a direct ride. The roads to the rest are the memorable part of the journey.

faq.q: How challenging are the roads to remote lighthouses?
faq.a: Often demanding. The B8007 to Ardnamurchan Point is a narrow, twisting single-track through remote wilderness, and the descent to the Mull of Kintyre lighthouse is extremely steep and among the most challenging in Scotland. Expect passing places, loose surfaces, and no barriers. Allow extra time, ride within your limits, and treat the journey as part of the reward.

faq.q: What should I prepare for at lighthouse headlands?
faq.a: Headlands are exposed, windswept, and offer no shelter, so brace for strong winds, especially approaching from the west. Many have no phone signal, so download offline maps before you set off. The roads to them are frequently single-track with passing places, which slows progress. Dress for cold, blustery conditions even on a mild day, as the coast is always cooler and gustier.

faq.q: When is the light best for lighthouse photography?
faq.a: Dawn and dusk are hard to beat, when low, warm light strikes the white towers and long shadows add depth. Neist Point in particular glows at sunset. Clear days give crisp Atlantic backdrops, while scattered cloud adds drama to the sky. Whatever the hour, place the tower against the sea and, if space allows, include your bike for scale and story.
